extracted.intended_audience: readers of Rabelais / readers of satirical, convivial Renaissance literature (self-described 'honest drinkers' and 'gouty gentlemen')
extracted.subtask_description: Writing/performing broad, bawdy, digressive satirical prose in the Rabelais tradition—addressed to a convivial readerly audience and mixing scatology, classical allusion, political satire, and exuberant hyperbole for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to make readers merry
rubrics_metrics.description: If you read them to make yourselves merry, as in manner of pastime I wrote them, you and I both are far more worthy of pardon than ... hypocrites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explicit purpose of the narratives is entertainment; frivolity and 'flimflam stories' are justified when aimed at merriment. The author defends light, comic writing as a legitimate activity and asks readers not to moralize it. Anti-pattern: treating comic/folly-oriented work as morally suspect simply because it is not solemn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address and target a specific convivial audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The prologue repeatedly invokes 'honest drinkers, most illustrious drinkers, thrice precious gouty gentlemen' as the intended readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declare and write for a concrete audience (convivial drinkers) so the tone, examples, and register align. The narrator restricts scope: 'I have not pierced this vessel for any else but you honest men.' Anti-pattern: trying to please all audiences at once; the author excludes hypocrites and pettifoggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack hypocrisy and dissemblers with satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical targets are named: 'squint-minded fellows, dissembling and counterfeit saints, demure lookers, hypocrites, pretended zealots, tough friars...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire to expose false piety, legal chicanery, and social pretense. The narrator encourages contempt for such figures and invites aggressive mockery. Example: direct vitriol and caricature of clerical hypocrisy. Scoring note: sharper, well-targeted ridicule is valued; bland or diffuse mockery is less effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ bawdy, scatological, and grotesque imagery for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of bodily functions and excremental imagery (hot piss, baths from Pantagruel's urine, montjoy of ordure, 'they made no more show in his mouth than a fart in yours').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earthy, bodily material is a deliberate comic device—used to shock, deflate pretension, and create comic grotesque. Examples throughout the healing episode and the narrator's jibes. Anti-pattern: sanitizing such material removes a central Rabelaisian energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extravagant hyperbole and absurd numeric/comic excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlandish exaggeration (e.g., transporting '9,876,543,210' Utopians; massive drug weights; giant copper balls) is a persistent technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy absurd, precise-seeming numbers and stupendous scales to produce ludicrous effect and satirize magnification. Hyperbole supports parody of authorities and systems. Anti-pattern: underplaying absurdity; literal realism contradicts the comic logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix learned/classical allusion with low comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent classical references (Diogenes, Homer, Virgil, Numa, Osiris, Ptolemy, Heraclitus) interwoven with rustic or scatological scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine erudition and ridicule: lofty citations juxtaposed with vulgar imagery enhances irony and satirizes pretension. Example: invoking philosophers while describing farting or ordure. Scoring note: the interplay of high and low registers is central; one without the other weakens the mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use long lists, catalogues, and rapid verb sequences for comic piling
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended catalogues (weapons, actions on the tub, list of thermal baths) and chains of verbs produce comic momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cataloguing and repetitive piling generate rhythm, excess, and mock-epic tone. Technique includes accumulation, variation, and comic verb strings. Anti-pattern: lists that are inert or purely decorative without rhetorical escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a roguish, conversational authorial persona
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narrator who sips wine, addresses readers, excuses faults, and claims a Diogenical identity—alternately self-deprecating and belligerent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An outspoken narrator persona (boastful, convivial, irreverent) mediates the satire and invites complicity. The persona both apologizes and boasts, framing transgressive humor as communal pastime. Example: narrator drinks, warns hypocrites, promises inexhaustible merriment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate benevolent, law-and-policy-based governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Political-normative claim: newly conquered peoples should be cherishingly governed—'Newborn, they must be given suck to, rocked ... Trees newly planted must be supported ...'—not oppressed by pillage and force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offering political satire, promote humane, legal, and beneficent policies as superior means of securing loyalty. Use historical examples (Osiris, Alexander, Numa) to justify gentle governance. Anti-pattern: endorsing tyranny or perpetual oppression as effective long-term policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow imperfection and shared human faults as comic ethos
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator admits imperfections in himself and readers: 'If he had some imperfection, so have you, so have we; for there is nothing, but God, that is perfect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge human frailty as part of the comic contract—self-mockery and mutual pardon make coarse humor socially permissible. This ethos softens attacks and fosters reader identification. Anti-pattern: moralizing condemnation that denies shared imperfection, which undermines the communal aspect of the humor.
